SR² Hand documentation · index of result pages · topic overview: printed fingertips and force sensing · updated 2026-10-21

Finite elements, magnetic readout and contact estimation of the printed TPU fingertips

The printed fingertip is a pad of Siraya Tech 85A TPU, two walls and four solid skins around a gyroid core, on the DIP link over ReSkin’s five-chip MLX90393 board, with five 3 × 2 mm magnets 7.5 mm under its apex. One chain of models follows it from the slicer’s rules to the chip readings: finite elements of the printed structure with the gyroid homogenized, the magnets’ motion under any surface load, and a field model of the five chips. Forward, the chain chose the design: concept b’s pad resolves 0.028–0.031 N per sample at its contact point with N52 magnets. Inverted, it estimates contact point and force anywhere on the pad from the 15 readings, 0.18 mm and 0.03 N median on simulated presses. No printed pad has yet been pressed against a force reference, and in the first presses by hand the pad moved in its seat.

Terms

Approach
Travel of a rigid indenter into the tip from first touch under a given normal force, in µm; the reference indenter is the 12.5 mm screwdriver shaft across the finger.
Wall, skin, core
The three printed structures: walls are the two 0.45 mm perimeters of every layer (0.9 mm, also around each magnet pocket), skins the four solid 0.2 mm layers under every top and bottom surface (0.8 mm), the core the gyroid infill.
Infill setting, solid fraction
The slicer’s gyroid density setting (30 or 50 %) and the volume fraction of TPU it prints, which differ because successive layers’ beads overlap only in part.
Homogenized tensor
The 6×6 elasticity tensor of a periodic cell of printed gyroid, per unit modulus of solid TPU : the stiffness of the core seen at the scale of the tip.
Contact modulus
The modulus of the sphere pads’ pressure law that best reproduces the FE approach at 0.5, 1 and 3 N, in MPa; the RL scenes use 10 MPa.
Magnet travel
Rigid motion of a magnet per newton of contact force, from the FE, in µm/N.
Sensing plane
The plane of the five chips’ Hall elements; on concept b it lies 0.42 mm below the pad’s back face.
Force resolution
The Cramér–Rao bound on the standard deviation of the pressing force from one conversion of the five chips (141 Hz) at a known contact point, with Earth’s field unknown, in N: the spread of the best unbiased estimate when the models are exact.
Sphere pads
The simulations’ contact model of the tip: 0.75 mm spheres on a 1 mm lattice over its surface, each with stiffness (builder v2: its depth below the tip’s volume centroid).
Rest calibration
The fit of the field model to the reading with the pad untouched: which chip address sits at which position, the chips’ axes, every magnet’s pole, the magnets’ strength and the pad’s offset on the board.
Sensitivity
The change of the 15 readings per newton of a patch load at surface point , along each axis of the tip frame (15×3).
Placed away
A simulated press whose estimated point lies more than 1.5 mm from the true one.
Tip frame
along the pad’s normal toward the palmar face, across the finger, from the mount toward the tip end, in mm.

Components of the fingertip and its models

The fingertip is concept b of the DIP-link study, chosen by the owner after the first prints of 2026-10-20: the front 13.45 of the 17.0 mm of the 11/22 half-ellipsoid tip of the simulations, printed as a pad that slides into a PLA cover on the DIP link over the ReSkin 5X board, whose chips lie 0.42 mm below the pad’s back face (DIP link b v3 and mount v2). Five N52 magnets, a centre one and four corners 7.4 mm apart, sit with their tops 7.5 mm under the apex, the shallowest depth that keeps 1.8 mm of TPU around every pocket. A press moves the magnets by a few micrometres; the chips read the change of their field.

Each box is one model with its own check. The finite elements resolve what the printer makes, walls, skins and gyroid, because the walls carry the face’s edges and set the patch the pads must reproduce. The field model represents each magnet as a cylinder of 72 dipoles, because one dipole is 5.5 % high at the chips’ distance. The rest calibration makes the chain usable on a pad as built: it finds the chips’ layout and the magnets’ poles and strength from 2 s of untouched reading. Forward, the chain ranks designs by their force resolution before anything is printed; inverted, it turns readings into a contact point and a force without a robot.

The printed pad

The pads print on the Prusa XL’s tool 2 or the P1S’s external spool in Siraya Tech 85A at 240 °C on a 35 °C bed, upright in 0.1 mm layers: two perimeters outside and around each pocket, four top and four bottom layers, gyroid at 30 or 50 %. The print pauses at 9.2 and 16.2 mm of height to take the magnets, north toward the palmar face, into pockets whose 2.9 mm seats hold them by press fit (the owner’s choice from the seat coupon, 2026-10-18). The recipe stays the same on every printer, so one FE describes every pad (print procedure). The pads weigh 0.6 % more TPU than the FE assumes, and concept a’s tips 3.0 % less, about 7 % softer (DIP link b v3 and mount v2).

85A at 30 % gyroid was chosen for the magnets’ travel: the softer the pad, the more field change per newton, until the approach outgrows what 1 mm pads represent. The rule from the co-design study is at least 12 µm/N of travel for 0.1 N (fingertip co-design); the 95A tips of the first studies gave 11.7 µm/N at best. eFlesh lattices travel 250 µm/N open, as eFlesh prints them, but sink 613 µm at 1 N and print with unsupported islands; closed by a skin on every face they sink 81 µm and give 0.075 N, the gyroid’s resolution (eFlesh printability).

Finite elements of the printed structure

Materials. The tip’s shape is voxelized at 0.05 mm. In each layer plane, TPU within 0.9 mm of the outline is wall; TPU within 0.8 mm of an exposed surface along the build axis is skin; the rest is core, and the magnets are a fourth class, with walls and skins lining their pockets as the slicer prints them. The classes are sampled onto a graded hexahedral grid, 0.2–0.25 mm under the face and 0.8–1.1 mm deep inside (about 120–220 thousand degrees of freedom). Walls and skins are solid TPU, isotropic with Poisson 0.45: 30 MPa for 95A and 12 MPa for 85A, from datasheets (NinjaFlex standing in for Siraya’s unmeasured 85A). The magnets are NdFeB at 160 GPa, bonded (finite elements of the printed tip).

Gyroid core. The core is homogenized from the gyroid as the slicer prints it. In each 0.2 mm layer the toolpath follows the zero set of the gyroid function at mid-layer with a 0.45 mm bead, and successive layers bond only where their beads overlap:

A periodic cell of these voxels takes six unit macroscopic strains ; each load case solves for the periodic fluctuation , and the effective tensor is the cell’s mean stress:

The result is orthotropic, stiffer along the build axis. At the settings used, 30 % prints 32.6 % solid with in the layer plane and along the build axis, and 50 % prints 55.0 % with 0.228 and 0.311; over 11–42 % solid and in the solid fraction , between the bending and stretching limits of Gibson and Ashby.

Tip model and contact. The elements are eight-node hexahedra with Wilson–Taylor incompatible modes, so the thin walls bend without shear locking (a 40-voxel cantilever comes out 2.4 % below beam theory, against 9.8 % for plain hexahedra); each takes the tensor of its class, the core’s rotated into the tip frame. Concept b’s pad is fixed at its cut face and the mount face. One sparse Cholesky factorization of is reused for every load. A rigid frictionless indenter (the shaft, a plate or a sphere) meets the face nodes, whose normal compliance comes from columns of ; at approach the nodal forces solve

and is bisected until equals the load. A magnet’s motion is the rigid fit of its nodes’ displacements. Each gap is measured from the tip’s analytic surface; on the curved tips the grid’s face nodes lie a median 0.10–0.13 mm from that surface (95th percentile 0.43–0.49 mm).

Solver. The solver is our own Python (scripts/tpu_tip_fem_core.py; SciPy, CHOLMOD and PyAMG on the CPU, PyTorch on the GPU). Its input is voxels, the slicer’s material classes at 0.05 mm or every gyroid bead at 0.1 mm, and on a voxel grid all elements of one size share one element matrix. The model resolving every bead, 1.7–2.2 million elements and 5–8 million degrees of freedom, is then solved matrix-free on the GPU in 2–3 GB and 60–140 s per approach. The off-the-shelf solvers installed for the study run on the CPU from tetrahedral meshes: FEniCSx took 3.3–5.7 GB for 0.45–0.68 million degrees of freedom of quadratic tetrahedra, a rate that puts the resolved tip above 40 GB on a 30 GB workstation, and PolyFEM’s IPC contact took 7–14 min for 57 thousand degrees of freedom. One element code also solves the periodic cells, the homogenized tip and the resolved tip, so their comparison tests the homogenization alone. FEniCSx and PolyFEM remain as checks (finite elements of the printed tip, Tables 7 and 8).

Checks. On the 95A block of the first study the model is 1.9 % off Hertz under a 40 mm sphere, and a model resolving every bead at 0.1 mm gives the homogenized tip’s approach within 2.6 % (44.8 against 46.0 µm at 1 N). On the 85A 11/22 tip and b’s pad the same check, 6–8 million degrees of freedom on the GPU, puts the resolved beads 1.6–4.8 % stiffer than the homogenized core under the rods and up to 7.8 % under a 2 mm sphere, about 1 % of it from the cell’s voxel size; a finer contact grid changes the approach by at most 3.6 % (v2 fingertip checks, Section 6; calibration to the finite elements). Solved from its G-code, pad B00 sinks 18 % less than the design pad under the rod at 1 N when its beads are drawn at their nominal widths, which put 11 % more TPU in the model than the printed parts weigh, and 3.9 % less with its TPU set to the weighed volume. Its 0.1 mm layers make the gyroid 8 % stiffer in the layer plane, and with that cell the homogenized pad agrees with the G-code model within 1 % under the rod (v2 fingertip checks). The G-code solve of the 95A tip of 10-13 read none of the G-code’s arc moves, 11 % of its filament; with them the tip sinks 33 against the design model’s 41 µm at 1 N, where the earlier reading gave 63 (eFlesh printability).

Effects of the design changes

Each change below was solved on the same models; approaches are under the 12.5 mm shaft at 1 N and resolutions per sample at the contact point (finite elements of the printed tip, v2 fingertip checks).

ChangeEffect
Infill, 85ASolid 20.2 µm ( 47.5 MPa); 50 % gyroid 43.3 µm (14.4); 30 % 74.7 µm (6.3) on the block; 95A at 20 % 46.0 µm
WallsCarry the face’s edges: 53 % of the load on the outer 1.2 mm of the 20 % tip, against 30 % for the pads’ law; twist arm 3.35 mm against the pads’ 2.72
Print deviationsPerimeters 10 % thinner +8.6 % approach; gyroid beads 10 % narrower +9.3 %; under-extrusion 5 or 10 % +8.7 or +19.6 %; skins 0.7 for 0.8 mm +0.05 %
Magnets as inclusionsFive 3 × 2 mm at 7.5 mm stiffen the 11/22 tip by 3.4 %; one 4.76 mm magnet 1.5, 3 or 5 mm deep in the 95A block by 99, 31 or 15 %
Five or four magnetsIn b’s pad at 7.5 mm: 0.0285 N with five, 0.0513 with four; five at 7.0 or 6.5 mm 0.0299 or 0.0308 (more travel, farther from the chips); at 8.5 mm the 41 mT field exceeds every gain
One perimeter per pocketFive magnets 0.0287 N, four 0.0460; travel 5.23 to 6.04 µm/N
Concept b against aThe cut pad of b: 2.5 % stiffer, 0.028 against 0.065 N, contact located to 0.34 × 0.42 against 1.40 × 1.31 mm, chips 3.5 mm closer
Cover walls on b’s flanksHeld both ways in the model (an upper bound): 3.0 mm walls −0.16 % approach and 0.030 N; v3’s 6 mm walls 0.0313 N; with the proposed tip cap 0.0317 N, with its side walls 0.0332 N
ShapeOf 24 printable fillet shapes none turns the tool better than the as-built block; curved tips cut the twist-onset arm to a third; in 85A at 30 % all shapes sink 251–262 µm under a 2 mm sphere

Two choices follow from the table: five magnets, because the centre magnet over U1 halves the resolution of four, and concept b, because the cut pad puts the magnets 3.5 mm closer to the chips. The cover walls and the cap cost at most 16 % of the resolution, in the bound that holds the flanks both ways.

Magnetic readout and force resolution

The ReSkin 5X board has five MLX90393 three-axis Hall magnetometers in a plus, U1 at the centre and U2–U5 7.00 mm from it; each chip senses 0.42 mm under its package top. A QT Py ESP32-S3 reads them over its STEMMA QT port in 2.0 ms, 375 records a second, while each chip converts every 7.0–7.1 ms (140–143 Hz). The firmware sets the gain at GAIN_SEL 1, RES 1 (1.20 µT a count on and , 1.94 on , a range of 38.4 mT), because b’s five magnets put 27.5 mT on the nearest chip and the most sensitive gain covers 4.8 mT. At rest the measured noise per sample is 1.54–1.76 µT on and and 2.32–2.59 µT on , 1.4 times the datasheet model for this gain. Three fingers’ boards answer at the same addresses and need an I²C multiplexer; a sweep of 15 chips takes 6.74 ms, inside one conversion (magnetometer readout, src/morphohand/driver/reskin5x/README.md).

The design studies rank layouts by force resolution. The FE gives each magnet’s translation and rotation per newton of a patch load; the field model turns that into the change of the 15 readings, the sensitivity ; and the noise bounds how well a force can be read. With a uniform background field (Earth’s) unknown, and the contact point too when it is unknown,

the Cramér–Rao bound on the pressing force from one sample. It is a lower bound: it assumes the models are exact. On the first 95A tip one 4.76 mm magnet 5 mm deep resolved 0.044 N at a known point and 0.08–1.48 N over the face when the point was unknown, which is why the layouts went to four magnets (0.14 N everywhere) and then five. On the 11/22 tip concept a resolves 0.065 N and b 0.028 N, with the contact located to 0.34 × 0.42 mm against a’s 1.40 × 1.31 mm; at the measured noise b’s 0.028 N becomes about 0.039 N (v2 fingertip checks).

The disturbances are larger than the noise. The chips run without their on-chip temperature compensation, and each one’s sensitivity falls by 0.65–0.70 % per °C of its die temperature: on the centre chip, in 7.6 mT, one degree is 53 µT, twice a 1 N press on the face, and the board warms by about 1 °C in the minutes after it is plugged in. Dividing each reading by its chip’s gain at the chip’s own temperature leaves 9 of those 70 µT (contact estimation, Section 9). On the first tip a facing fingertip’s magnet moving from 25 to 30 mm read as 5.16 N, 2.01 N with the field’s gradient estimated; the hand’s joint angles give the other magnets’ positions, so their field can be subtracted. Earth’s field, 1.71 N on U1 alone, drops out of the five-chip estimate. The board must not move against the pad: on concept a with four magnets, 1 µm of board motion reads as 0.160 N, which is why the board is clamped (DIP link board mount).

Contact point and force from the readings

The estimator runs the chain backwards (contact estimation). At rest the 15 components are the magnets’ field and Earth’s. With each chip’s rotation taken from the board’s pick-and-place file and one common offset fitted, the rest calibration finds which address sits at which position, every magnet’s pole, the magnets’ strength and the pad’s offset on the board. On pad B00 as first assembled it fits at 0.43 mT RMS against fields of 1.9–7.0 mT, and finds magnets at 35 % of an N52’s moment with two diagonal corners reversed, which the owner confirmed were not N52 and inserted at random. A press then changes the reading by

where comes from an FE basis of 1 N loads along , and at the 812 pad points over the whole free surface (2,436 load cases, 101 s, 2.0 GB), interpolated between them by a thin-plate spline, and holds a uniform field change and a strength change with Gaussian priors. With the covariance of the noise and the nuisance terms and a force prior  N, the force at each candidate point and the point itself follow from

the log marginal likelihood of a contact at , over 12,581 candidate points about 0.2 mm apart, with the force pressing, inside a friction cone of 2 and below 25 N. The determinant charges each point for the patterns it could explain: without it the best fit often went to a flank point where the reading barely responds, with forces of 100 N and more. The Fisher information gives each estimate’s 1-sigma; one estimate takes 1.2 ms.

On 600 simulated presses with N52 magnets and the 50 ms window, 2 % are placed more than 1.5 mm away; the rest have median errors of 0.20 mm and 0.036 N on the face and 0.17 mm and 0.050 N on the flanks, and the errors follow the predicted 1-sigma (ratio 1.10–1.16). With the magnets in the pad today, 15 % are placed away and the rest have 0.39 mm and 0.08 N. Over 30 s without a press, one frame of 880 shows a contact.

The fingertip in the simulations

The simulations represent the tip by sphere pads, 0.75 mm spheres on a 1 mm lattice over its surface, each with stiffness ; builder v2, the default since 2026-10-15, takes as each pad’s depth below the tip’s volume centroid. One modulus misses the FE’s approach by 20–28 %, because the FE’s force grows as and the law’s as : the walls and skins spread the load over the core. A stiff local modulus behind a series spring, with  N/mm, fits the 11/22 tip within 5.2 % RMS approach in Drake’s hydroelastic field and 5.6 % in 0.5 mm pads, though no single spring fits the capsule (calibration to the finite elements). With the spring in both simulators, the same servo commands end the tool’s turn 6.3° apart in place of 18.6°, while their contact forces still differ by 0.37 N against a 0.25 N bound (v2 fingertip checks). The estimator reports its forces at the same pads the simulations use, so a measured contact and a simulated one can be compared pad by pad.

Hardware built and measured

The DIP link holds the board against the pad. Of three concepts, the window plate with a clamp (a), a cover that clamps the board behind the pad on rails (b) and a board printed over (c), the design judge chose a on 2026-10-18 and the owner took a and b to print; on 2026-10-20 the owner chose b (“concept B is the clear winner”), which also resolves 0.028 against 0.065 N. Version 2 keeps the board’s own Qwiic connector and lays the cable in a groove past the slotted arm, with both links 9.75 mm longer; v3 adds 6 mm cover walls along the pad’s flanks, a column under the pad and a cable leg open to the top (DIP link board mount, DIP link b v3 and mount v2).

In the prints of 2026-10-20 the rails at groove fit B00 slot together but pop off under a sideways push, and cover W00 keeps pad B00 in place. In the owner’s first presses by hand the pad rocked in its seat: after the fourth and fifth presses the reading stayed 62 and 104 µT from rest, which a rigid shift of the whole pad by 17–23 µm with a tilt of about 4 mrad reproduces (7–14 % residual, 62 % for random patterns), and which the estimator reads as standing contacts of 11–12 N. The owner accepted a cap over the tip end the same evening: an end plate on the pad’s flat end, ears under the two distal board screws and a 2 mm pin into the pad (pad B00P has its hole), with 6 mm side walls on the distal flanks in variant TW; in the FE bound the plate and pin cost 1 % of the resolution and the side walls 6 %, and both caps print in 17 min (DIP link board mount).

On 2026-10-21, before the cap, touches still moved the rest by 33–69 µT (rigid shifts of 8–19 µm), and over a night at rest the estimator with the chips’ noise alone showed a contact 95 % of the time, from the 8–14 µT of drift that the temperature correction and the estimator’s nuisances leave. The viewer now adds a noise floor of 2 µT to every component, shows a contact only above 0.25 N and takes a new baseline once the reading has been as still as at rest for 3 s: no contact shows at rest over the night or the board’s warm-up, the smallest press shown on the face rises from 0.20 to 0.60 N, and a press held still for 3 s goes into the baseline (contact estimation, Section 9).

The UR5e calibration mount clamps the DIP link to the OnRobot HEX-E with the finger along the tool axis, so the normal force falls on the sensor’s lateral axes (noise 0.035 N against 0.15 N axially); under 10 N the HEX-E deflects 0.49 mm, the link 0.010–0.026 mm and the mount 0.004 mm. The first version printed with a spigot the HEX-E has no bore for and a key that snapped; v2 clocks the link by walls around its legs and homes on a drafted key on each indenter, and is sliced but not all printed (UR5e mount v1). The UR5e and the HEX-E are connected to the lab’s computer, which this workstation cannot reach.

Open questions

  1. The force scale. No printed pad has been pressed against a force reference. The FE takes Siraya 85A at 12 MPa from a NinjaFlex datasheet (95A datasheets span 26–67 MPa), every force scales with that modulus, and the G-code solves put the printed pads 4–18 % stiffer than the design model, depending on how much TPU the beads hold. A scale or load cell under a printed indenter settles the scale; an indentation with the HEX-E separates the pad’s stiffness from the magnets’ strength.
  2. The seat. The FE fixes the pad’s cut face, and the pad as assembled moved 17–23 µm and stayed there; touches on 2026-10-21 still moved it 8–19 µm. The viewer’s re-zero at rest clears the offsets but takes in a press held still for 3 s. The tip cap is meant to hold the pad; until it returns to its seat within a few µT after a firm press, neither the model nor a UR5e calibration describes it.
  3. The magnets. The N52 magnets are on order. Today’s resolve 0.10–0.12 N; with N52 all one way the models predict 0.028–0.031 N, about 0.039 N at the measured noise. Four magnets (0.051 N) or five (0.029 N) waits on the owner; a test of pads B4 and B00 measures the ratio, predicted 1.8.
  4. Disturbances in the hand. The other fingers’ magnets (5.16 N equivalent at 25–30 mm on the first tip) and steel near the pad are modelled but not measured. The chips’ temperature drift is measured, 0.65–0.70 % per °C, and the correction from each chip’s temperature leaves 9 of 70 µT over a warm-up; the magnets’ own coefficient, which follows the pad’s lagging temperature, is not separated yet.
  5. Large presses and shear. The FE is linear and frictionless; a neo-Hookean check lost 11 % of the force at 350 µm on the softest tip. The tip’s tangential compliance, 48–177 µm/N, is in neither simulator, and the estimator’s shear has not been tested.
  6. The simulators. Calibrated to the FE, the pads and Drake agree on approach within 6 % but end a turn 6.3° apart with contact forces 0.37 N apart; whether builder v2 stays the default waits on the owner.

Future work

  1. Seat: with the pad fastened, record five firm presses with 2 s rests and run src/morphohand/driver/reskin5x/host/pad_shift_check.py; every rest within 5 µT of the first passes (0.2 N on the face), offsets of tens of µT that a rigid motion fits mean the pad still moves.
  2. N52 magnets: recalibrate in the viewer (key c); a strength of 0.8–1.2, all poles one way and a rest residual below 0.43 mT confirm the field model; a lower strength or larger residual means the magnets’ depth or the pad’s seat differs from the FE.
  3. Force reference without the UR5e: a kitchen scale or load cell under a printed indenter, holds at about 1, 2 and 4 N at the face centre, a flank and the tip end; an estimated press more than three model sigmas from the reference falsifies the force scale at that point, and the ratio refits .
  4. Indentation with the HEX-E: approach against force at 0.5, 1 and 3 N under the 12.5 mm rod, from first touch. At 1 N the design model of b’s pad gives 185 µm and B00’s G-code model with its TPU as weighed 178 µm (v2 fingertip checks, Table 5); outside ±25 % of both falsifies the pad’s modelled stiffness, independently of the magnets, and points at the datasheet modulus. A result nearer the G-code model moves the calibration to the 0.1 mm-layer cell (case b_v2_cl01).
  5. Sensing rows on the probes’ gap rule: run_sense in scripts/v2_tip_fe_checks.py takes its gaps from tpu_tip_magnet.gaps, which moves a face node onto the analytic surface only within half a grid cell of it, and gives 150 against the probe rows’ 185 µm for the same pad at 1 N. Rerun --sense b_v2 with every face node on the surface; a force resolution that moves by more than 5 % means the DIP page’s resolutions need the same rerun.
  6. UR5e session on the lab’s computer: probe points from the basis’s pad points over the face and both flanks, three normal forces and two shear directions each, a return to one reference point every ten presses, 30 s rests; refit strength, offsets, , and per-magnet strengths on half the points and compare the other half’s errors with the model 1-sigma.
  7. Facing finger: record the board with a second tip’s magnets at 20–40 mm and compare with the dipole prediction before subtracting it from the joint angles.
  8. Temperature: with the pad at rest, hold a warm hand around the finger for 60 s and take it away, with the viewer logging, and run scripts/fingertip_contact_estimation_study.py thermal on that stretch: no contact should show while the chips warm by 2–3 °C. A drift that grows with the temperature after the correction means the magnets need a coefficient of their own; firmware with TCMP_EN 1 is the alternative to test the same way.

2026-10-21Spherical and disc N52 magnets in the B00 fingertip padA 3 mm N52 sphere resolves 0.0285 N on pad B00 against 0.0304 N for the 3 x 2 mm disc of equal volume; spheres of 4 mm and more exceed the MLX90393's range at the five-magnet centres, and four 4 mm spheres on the four-magnet layout resolve 0.023 N if their walls pass.
2026-10-21DIP link b v4 and a sweep of retaining-wall heightsDIP link b v4 recesses the bridge's palmar edge to x_F -6.46 mm and shrinks the column under the pad, so a flat object meets the pad 4.0 mm before any rigid part (v3: 0.0 mm); the joint still stops on the horn arm at 93.0 deg. Covers I15 with 4, 3 and 2 mm walls and caps with 4, 3 and 2 mm blocks at 0.15 mm went to the owner's height test; the owner chose 3 mm, and the set of 2026-10-22 adds rails 0.10-0.16 mm tighter per flank and a 1.6 mm pin hole.
2026-10-19Print sheet for the fit tests of DIP-link concept b, 19 October 2026Two plates print the fit tests of DIP-link concept b, v2 (the link 9.75 mm longer, the Qwiic cable turned toward the back at the plug and routed past the slotted arm): 8 PLA pieces on the Bambu Lab P1S as one sliced Bambu Studio project (1 h 9 min, 18.3 g) and 5 Siraya Tech 85A groove blocks on one Bambu Lab P1S plate with the other run’s 85A blocks, from the external spool (26 min, 4.2 g for all 12).
2026-10-19Print sheet for the DIP-link fit tests of 19 October 2026Two plates print every fit test of DIP-link concept a, v2 (the link 9.75 mm longer, with the Qwiic cable routed past the slotted arm): 12 PLA pieces on the Bambu Lab P1S as one sliced Bambu Studio project (2 h 10 min, 31.1 g) and 7 Siraya Tech 85A channel blocks on one Bambu Lab P1S plate with the other run’s 85A blocks, from the external spool (26 min, 4.2 g for all 12).
2026-10-18Calibration mount for the instrumented DIP link on a UR5e and HEX-EThree PLA parts clamp a DIP link as printed (the CAD hand's, or v2 a or b of the DIP study, which keep its clevis arms within 0.01 mm) to the tool plate of an OnRobot HEX-E QC on the UR5e, so that the five magnetometers can be calibrated against the HEX-E.Link
2026-10-16Deployment readiness of the CAD hand with printed 85A magnet fingertipsPrinted in Siraya Tech 85A at 30 % gyroid, the four-magnet fingertip block behaves on the hand’s tasks as the modelled TPU block did: the eight deployed bench plans keep the tool in 24 of 24 replays, within 1.9° RMS of Drake, and the four D6 policies hold it in 64 of 64 rollouts; capsule and half-ellipsoid tips drop it.Link
